result.markdown: --- title: "Open, Replicable, and Ethical Science" subtitle: "Course 2 (ORES) · planning studies that justify their inferences" --- A hands-on course that teaches tools still rarely used in behavioural research. It draws on Daniël Lakens' open teaching materials (e.g., *Improving Your Statistical Inferences*) and the R package rpact. ## Topics - **Preregistration and registered reports**, including for observational field data and secondary analyses. - **Sequential analyses:** group-sequential designs with planned interim analyses and alpha spending, so data collection can stop early for efficacy without inflating the type I error. - **Optional stopping and stopping for futility:** why peeking at *p*-values inflates error rates (shown by simulation), and how to stop correctly, including when an effect is unlikely to emerge. ::: {.box} **Why this matters at DPZ:** sequential designs and stopping for futility reduce the expected number of animals per study. This directly supports the *Reduction* principle of the 3Rs and strengthens the justification in animal-ethics applications. ::: **Outcome:** each participant drafts a preregistration with a sample-size or sequential plan for their own project. ::: {.key-terms} **Key terms:** [Preregistration](../glossary.qmd#preregistration), [Registered report](../glossary.qmd#registered-report), [Sequential analysis](../glossary.qmd#sequential-analysis), [Alpha spending](../glossary.qmd#alpha-spending), [Optional stopping](../glossary.qmd#optional-stopping), [Stopping for futility](../glossary.qmd#stopping-for-futility), [3Rs](../glossary.qmd#three-rs) ::: ## Simulate first: why peeking is a problem There is **no effect** in these simulations. A researcher tests after every 10 observations per group and stops as soon as *p* < .05. How often do they find a "significant" result? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(12) looks <- seq(10, 100, by = 10) nsim <- 2000 first_sig <- replicate(nsim, { a <- rnorm(max(looks)); b <- rnorm(max(looks)) # H0 is true p <- sapply(looks, function(n) t.test(a[1:n], b[1:n])$p.value) which(p < .05)[1] # first look with p < .05 (NA if none) }) alpha_by_look <- sapply(seq_along(looks), function(k) mean(!is.na(first_sig) & first_sig <= k)) plot(looks, alpha_by_look, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#c0392b", ylim = c(0, .25), xlab = "Maximum n per group (one look every 10)", ylab = "Type I error rate") abline(h = .05, lty = 2, col = "#1b6f8a") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){width=975} ::: ::: With ten looks, the false-positive rate is far above the nominal 5 %. Group-sequential designs (e.g., with `rpact`) fix this by spending the alpha across the planned looks. ## Materials ::: {.materials} - Slides coming soon - R scripts coming soon - Preregistration template coming soon ::: ## Reading and tools - Lakens, D. *Improving your statistical inferences.* - Lakens, D. (2022). Sample size justification. *Collabra: Psychology, 8*(1), 33267. - R package: [rpact](https://www.rpact.org/) [Testing predictions of "no effect" is the topic of a separate course: [Testing for Absence and Equivalence](../tae/index.qmd).]{.muted}
